content.equation:
Creatinine Clearance (Clcr)
Note: Calculation uses actual body weight to calculate for Clcr; therefore, in obese patients (and possibly patients with ascites) Clcr may be
significantly overestimated. Some clinicians may prefer to use an adjusted body weight in such cases [eg, IBW + 0.4 (ABW - IBW)]. Patients
with estimated Clcr ≥60 mL/minute and actual weight <130% of IBW may be candidates for once daily dosing. Use clinical judgment.
Cockcroft-Gault Method:
Male: Clcr = [(140 - age) x weight] ÷ (72 x SrCr)
Female: Clcr = [(140 - age) x weight] ÷ [(72 x SrCr)] x 0.85
Clcr = estimated creatinine clearance in mL/min
Age is input in years
Weight is input in kg
SrCr = serum creatinine input in mg/dL
Jelliffe Method:
Male: Clcr = [98 - 0.8 x (age - 20)] ÷ SrCr
Female: Clcr = ([98 - 0.8 x (age - 20)] ÷ SrCr) x 0.90
Clcr = estimated creatinine clearance in mL/min/1.73 m2
Age is input in years
SrCr = serum creatinine input in mg/dL
Weight Factor (WF):
Ideal Body Weight (IBW):
Male: IBW = 50 + [2.3 x (height - 60)]
Female: IBW = 45.5 + [2.3 x (height - 60)]
IBW = ideal body weight in kg
Height measured in inches
Adjusted Body Weight (ABW):
ABW = IBW + [0.4 x (weight - IBW)]
WF = weight (if weight < IBW)
WF = IBW (if IBW < weight < 120% of IBW
WF = ABW (if weight > 120% of IBW)
Dose:
Dose (mg) = WF x Dose (mg/kg)
Interval:
Clcr ≥60 mL/min or mL/min/1.73 m2: 24 hours
Clcr 40-59 mL/min or mL/min/1.73 m2: 36 hours
Clcr 30-39 mL/min or mL/min/1.73 m2: 48 hours
Clcr <30 mL/min or mL/min/1.73 m2: Use conventional dosing

content.instructions: To perform a calculation, enter the required variables. Once all the inputs are entered, click the "Calculate" button to perform the calculation. Any time an input variable is adjusted, the "Calculate" button must be clicked to populate the new output. To start over, click the "Reset" button to clear all values and begin the calculation again. Aminoglycosides are antibiotics commonly used to treat serious bacterial infections. They distribute well into synovial, peritoneal, ascitic, and pleural fluids, but poorly into CNS and the vitreous humor of eye. They are eliminated rapidly by the kidneys. Traditionally, aminoglycoside antibiotics have been administered in multiple daily doses (aka, conventional dosing). An alternative approach to dosing these agents involves achieving higher peak concentrations and using an extended dosing interval. This strategy is often referred to as “extended interval dosing”, “single daily dosing”, or “once daily dosing”. The rationale behind extended interval dosing includes: Post-antibiotic effect (PAE): Aminoglycosides exhibit significant bacterial growth inhibition even after drug concentrations fall to undetectable levels. Concentration dependent killing: The bactericidal activity of aminoglycosides requires a high peak/MIC ratio. Adaptive post-exposure resistance: More frequent dosing may result in reduced bacterial uptake of aminoglycosides; thereby, increasing the MIC. Extended interval dosing may allow for the preservation of lower MICs. Reduced emergence of resistant organisms: Achieving drug concentrations 8-10x the MIC may reduce the emergence of drug resistant organisms. Impact on toxicities: The use of extended interval dosing has been shown to result in equal or less nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity when compared to conventional dosing. In theory, the rate of uptake of aminoglycosides into the renal cortex and vestibular and cochlear tissues is saturable. Therefore, the efficiency of aminoglycoside uptake into these tissues may be reduced when higher doses are given less frequently. The use of extended interval dosing is controversial and may not be appropriate for all patients; use clinical judgment. Settings in which conventional dosing may be more appropriate include clinical states characterized by: Rapid clearance of aminoglycosides: Patients with extensive burns (>20% of body surface area) Patients with sepsis and well-preserved renal function Patients with cystic fibrosis (Note: Extended interval dosing may be appropriate in these patients; higher doses are required) Variable pharmacokinetics: Neonates Patients with ascites Patients with anasarca Miscellaneous: Patients with enterococcal endocarditis Pregnant patients Pediatric patients Patients with severe renal disease (Clcr <30 mL/min) Neutropenic patients Patients with Gram-positive infections where the aminoglycoside is being used for synergy Patients with a history of allergy to aminoglycosides Patients with a history or signs of hearing loss or vestibular dysfunction The dosing interval should be adjusted based on a random level taken several hours after the end of the infusion using one of several interval adjustment nomograms (see Aminoglycosides: Extended Interval Dosing, Interval Adjustment).
